title: Tested in the Wilderness, Light in Galilee
summary: Led by the Spirit into the wilderness, Jesus fasts forty days and forty nights and is tempted by the devil three times, answering each temptation with words Moses spoke to Israel in Deuteronomy 6 to 8. After John's arrest Jesus withdraws to Galilee and settles in Capernaum, which Matthew reads as the dawning of the light Isaiah promised to Zebulun, Naphtali, and Galilee of the nations. He begins to preach that the kingdom of heaven is near, calls two pairs of fishermen to follow him, and goes throughout Galilee teaching, preaching, and healing, while crowds gather from every side.
story:
At the Jordan the Father declared, “This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (3:17). The very next sentence puts that sonship to the test. Israel had been called God's firstborn son at the exodus (Exodus 4:22), passed through the sea, and then spent forty years in the wilderness, where it hungered and grumbled for bread, put God to the test at Massah, and bowed to a golden calf. Matthew has already applied Hosea's words about Israel, “Out of Egypt I called My Son”, to the child Jesus (2:15). Now the Son who has passed through the water spends forty days and forty nights in the wilderness, and where Israel failed he holds firm, answering the tempter with the words Moses spoke to Israel about those same wilderness years. The devil comes as the tempter and leaves defeated; angels come and serve the Son.

The second half of the chapter moves from the lonely wilderness to the crowded lakeshore. John the Baptist's arrest marks a turning point: the forerunner is silenced and Jesus steps forward. Matthew places the start of the public ministry in Galilee, a borderland with a long memory of conquest, and reads it through Isaiah's promise of light for those who sat in darkness. With the words “From that time on Jesus began to preach” (verse 17), a formula Matthew repeats only at 16:21 when Jesus begins to speak of his suffering, the Gospel turns from who Jesus is to what he proclaims. The pattern of the ministry is set in a few verses: the announcement of the kingdom, the call of disciples who leave everything, and a summary of teaching, preaching, and healing (verse 23) that Matthew will repeat almost word for word at 9:35. Between those two summaries stand the Sermon on the Mount (chapters 5 to 7) and ten mighty works (chapters 8 and 9), so that the end of this chapter is the doorway to the Messiah of word and the Messiah of deed.
historical:
The chapter's setting is the late 20s AD. Galilee and Perea were ruled by Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great, as tetrarch under Rome from 4 BC to AD 39, while Judea and Jerusalem were under the Roman prefect Pontius Pilate (about AD 26 to 36). Matthew says only that Jesus heard that John ‘had been handed over’ (paredothē, verse 12); the full story comes in 14:3-12. Josephus, writing in the 90s, independently reports that Antipas imprisoned John at the fortress of Machaerus east of the Dead Sea and executed him because he feared that John's hold on the crowds might lead to revolt (Antiquities 18.116-119). The verb Matthew uses for John's arrest is the one he will use for Jesus being handed over to death (17:22, 20:18-19, 26:2), and Jesus ‘withdrew’ (anechōrēsen), a verb Matthew uses ten times, often of stepping back from danger (2:12-14, 2:22, 12:15, 14:13). Galilee was Antipas's territory too, so the move was not an escape from his reach but a choice of where to begin.

Matthew's quotation of Isaiah recalls a specific catastrophe. In the Syro-Ephraimite crisis of 734 to 732 BC the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser III took “Ijon, Abel-beth-maacah, Janoah, Kedesh, Hazor, Gilead, and Galilee, including all the land of Naphtali” and deported the population (2 Kings 15:29). Assyrian administrative records show the conquered territory reorganized into provinces, and many historians match Isaiah's three phrases to them: the Way of the Sea to the coastal province of Dor, beyond the Jordan to Gilead, and Galilee of the nations to the province of Megiddo, which took in the Galilean hills. Zebulun and Naphtali were therefore the first of Israel's lands to fall into darkness, and Isaiah promised that they would be the first to see the light (Isaiah 9:1-2). The Hebrew phrase gelil haggoyim means ‘the district of the nations’; gelil, a circle or ring, is the root of the name Galilee.

By Jesus' day the phrase was still apt but no longer describes a Gentile majority. First Maccabees 5:15 speaks of ‘all Galilee of the foreigners’ joining against the Jews in the 160s BC, when Judas Maccabeus's brother Simon brought the Jews of Galilee to Judea for safety (5:21-23). The Hasmonean rulers annexed Galilee around 104 BC; Josephus says Aristobulus I compelled part of the Iturean people to be circumcised and live by Jewish law (Antiquities 13.318-319). Archaeology of the early Roman period shows Galilean villages with stepped immersion pools, stone vessels, and an absence of pig bones, the marks of a Jewish population, and Mark Chancey (The Myth of a Gentile Galilee, 2002) has argued that the region was overwhelmingly Jewish in Jesus' time. Yet it was ringed by Gentile territory: the Phoenician cities of Tyre and Sidon to the northwest, the Decapolis to the southeast, and Philip's largely non-Jewish tetrarchy to the northeast. Matthew's Galilee of the Gentiles is a Jewish land at the edge of the nations, which fits a Gospel that ends with the command to disciple all the nations (28:19).

Capernaum, which Matthew later calls Jesus' ‘own town’ (9:1), lay on the northwest shore of the lake near the border between the territories of Antipas and Philip. Matthew locates it ‘in the region of Zebulun and Naphtali’ (verse 13) to fit Isaiah's words; strictly it lay in Naphtali's old allotment. The excavations there, described in the notes on Mark 1 and Luke 4, show a modest lakeside town of basalt houses. Josephus describes the lake as 140 stadia long and 40 wide (roughly 26 by 7 kilometers; modern measurements give about 21 by 13), with sweet water and many kinds of fish, and names a spring called Capharnaum that watered the plain of Gennesaret (Jewish War 3.506-521).

The Decapolis (verse 25) was a league of Greek cities. Pliny the Elder, writing in the 70s, lists ten of them, among them Scythopolis, Hippos, Gadara, Pella, Gerasa, Philadelphia, and Damascus, noting that authors do not all give the same list (Natural History 5.74). All lay east of the Jordan except Scythopolis. ‘Syria’ in verse 24 is either the Roman province of Syria, which bordered Galilee to the north and to which Judea was attached, or the wider region north of Galilee; many scholars think Matthew himself wrote in Syria, perhaps at Antioch, which may be why only this Gospel mentions it here.
cultural:
Forty days and forty nights is Matthew's wording (Mark and Luke say forty days), and it matches the Greek of Moses' fast on Sinai, when he was with the LORD “forty days and forty nights without eating bread or drinking water” (Exodus 34:28; compare Deuteronomy 9:9, 18), and Elijah's walk to Horeb, the mountain of God, in the strength of food given by an angel (1 Kings 19:8). Moses and Elijah are the two figures who later appear with Jesus on the mountain of transfiguration (17:3). A fast of this length was a mark of a prophet at the threshold of revelation, and the hunger that follows (verse 2) makes the first temptation a real one.

Jewish thought about Satan had developed across the Old Testament and the centuries after it. In Job 1 and 2 and Zechariah 3 the satan, ‘the adversary’ or ‘the accuser’, is a member of the heavenly court who tests and accuses; 1 Chronicles 21:1 uses Satan as a name for the one who incited David to sin. Later Jewish writings give him many names: Mastema in Jubilees, Belial in the Dead Sea Scrolls, where the Community Rule speaks of the dominion of Belial over the present age. Matthew uses three names in eleven verses: the devil (diabolos, the Septuagint's rendering of satan, ‘slanderer’), the tempter (ho peirazōn, verse 3), and Satan (verse 10). Jewish tradition also knew that God tests those he loves. The Mishnah says Abraham was tested with ten trials and stood firm in them all, and that Israel's ancestors tested God ten times in the wilderness (m. Avot 5:3-4, drawing on Numbers 14:22). The story of Jesus' testing belongs to that world: the righteous are tried, and Israel's failure in the wilderness is the pattern to be reversed.

The pinnacle of the temple (to pterugion, ‘the little wing’) was some high point of Herod's vast temple complex, probably an edge or corner of the outer walls; Josephus says that anyone looking down from the Royal Portico along the southern side into the Kidron valley grew dizzy (Antiquities 15.411-412). The word appears in an early Christian memory of James the brother of Jesus: Hegesippus, a second-century writer quoted by Eusebius (Church History 2.23), says the scribes and Pharisees set James on the pterugion of the temple so that the people could hear him, and then threw him down. Whatever its exact location, the place was public, sacred, and dangerous, and a leap from it would have been a spectacle in the holy city.

The devil's offer of all the kingdoms of the world and their glory (verse 8) had a concrete face in Jesus' world. Herod the Great, who rebuilt the Jerusalem temple, also built temples to Rome and Augustus: at Sebaste in Samaria, at Caesarea on the coast, where Josephus says a colossal statue of Augustus stood beside one of Roma (Antiquities 15.339), and at Panion near the springs of the Jordan (Antiquities 15.363-364), close to the Galilee where Jesus would preach. Worship of the emperor as a divine benefactor was spreading across the eastern provinces. An offer of empire in exchange for worship was therefore not an abstraction: it was the bargain the rulers of Jesus' own land had made.

Disciples in the Jewish world normally chose their teacher (m. Avot 1:6); here, as in Mark, Jesus chooses and calls. The two nets in the story differ: Simon and Andrew are casting an amphiblēstron (verse 18), a circular throw net flung from the shore or the shallows, while James and John are mending diktya (verse 21), the larger nets worked from a boat. Zebedee's family owned a boat and, in Mark's telling, employed hired men (Mark 1:20). In a world where sons carried on the family trade and owed their fathers honor and support in old age, leaving ‘the boat and their father’ (verse 22) was a costly break. Fish from the lake were salted and traded widely; the lakeside town of Magdala was known in Greek as Taricheae, from the word for salted fish.

The illnesses in verse 24 are named as ancient people named them. Those ‘suffering acute pain’ translates basanois, torments; the ‘demon-possessed’ are daimonizomenoi; those ‘having seizures’ translates selēniazomenoi, literally ‘moonstruck’, a word that reflects the ancient belief that the moon caused epilepsy and is the root of the old English word lunatic. Matthew uses it only here and at 17:15, where the father describes his son's convulsions. The list distinguishes illness from possession, as the Gospels usually do, and the summary insists that Jesus healed them all.
literary:
The chapter has two halves joined by a hinge. The temptation (verses 1 to 11) is a contest in three rounds, each built the same way: the devil's challenge, then Jesus' reply introduced by ‘it is written’ (gegraptai, a perfect tense, ‘it stands written’). All three replies come from Deuteronomy 6 to 8, the section in which Moses reflects on Israel's testing: Deuteronomy 8:3 on bread, 6:16 on Massah, and 6:13 on worshiping God alone. In the first two rounds the devil begins “If You are the Son of God”, a conditional that assumes the title the Father has just spoken and invites Jesus to prove it on the devil's terms; in the third he drops the title and asks for worship outright. In the second round the devil quotes Scripture himself (Psalm 91:11-12), leaving out the words “to guard you in all your ways”, so that the Bible becomes the tempter's instrument. The scene rises in height and in stakes: from a stony wilderness to the pinnacle of the temple to a very high mountain, and from bread to spectacle to worship. It ends where the Gospel will end, on a mountain, with the question of authority over all the kingdoms answered: here Jesus refuses the kingdoms from the devil, and in 28:16-20 he receives all authority in heaven and on earth from the Father, on a mountain in Galilee.

Matthew's order (bread, temple, mountain) differs from Luke's (bread, mountain, temple). Matthew marks the sequence with ‘then’ (tote, verse 5) and ‘again’ (palin, verse 8), while Luke uses only ‘and’; Luke's order ends in Jerusalem, the city toward which his whole Gospel moves. Most scholars think Matthew preserves the earlier order and Luke rearranged it, but the question is open, and the Luke note in this Study Bible sets out the case. Jesus' dismissal, “Away from Me, Satan” (hypage, Satana), anticipates his rebuke of Peter at Caesarea Philippi, “Get behind Me, Satan” (16:23), when Peter urges him away from the cross: the same temptation to a kingdom without suffering comes back through a friend.

The second half (verses 12 to 25) is a transition built from four blocks: a movement and a fulfillment quotation (12 to 16), a summary of preaching (17), a call story told twice in parallel (18 to 22), and a summary of ministry (23 to 25). The quotation of Isaiah is the fifth of Matthew's ten or so formula quotations introduced by ‘to fulfill what was spoken through the prophet’, and it is the only one in chapters 3 to 7. The two call scenes are deliberately matched: Jesus sees two brothers; they are at work with nets; he calls; ‘at once’ or ‘immediately’ they leave (nets in the first scene, boat and father in the second) and follow. Jesus' message in verse 17 repeats word for word the Baptist's in 3:2, and the disciples will preach the same in 10:7, so one proclamation passes from John to Jesus to the Twelve. The summary of verse 23, teaching, preaching, healing, is repeated almost exactly in 9:35, and the two verses bracket the Sermon on the Mount and the ten miracles of chapters 8 and 9, the Messiah's word and the Messiah's deed. Jack Dean Kingsbury (Matthew: Structure, Christology, Kingdom, 1975) argued that the phrase ‘from that time Jesus began’ at 4:17 and 16:21 divides the Gospel into three parts; others, following Benjamin Bacon's older proposal, organize it around five great discourses, the first of which begins in the next chapter. Both observations help: 4:17 opens the public proclamation, and 4:23-25 gathers the audience for the first discourse.

outline.t: The first test: stones into bread
The second test: the pinnacle of the temple
The third test: all the kingdoms of the world
Jesus moves to Capernaum and preaches the kingdom
The call of the first disciples
Teaching, preaching, and healing throughout Galilee

doctrines.note: Jesus relives Israel's story and succeeds where Israel failed. Forty days answer forty years; every reply comes from Moses' words about Israel's testing (Deuteronomy 8:2-3, 6:13, 6:16). Matthew presents him as the faithful Son in whom Israel's vocation is fulfilled, not as a replacement for Israel but as its true representative, who then gathers a renewed people beginning with two pairs of Galilean brothers.

The final temptation strips the contest to its core: “fall down and worship me”. Jesus answers with Deuteronomy 6:13, “Worship the Lord your God and serve Him only.” Worship belongs to God alone, and it cannot be traded for power, success, or safety. Matthew's verb for worship (proskyneō) is also used of the Magi (2:11) and the disciples (14:33, 28:17) bowing before Jesus, which he accepts.

Jesus refuses the kingdoms of the world when offered by the devil and then announces that the kingdom of heaven, God's own reign, has come near (verse 17). He shows what the kingdom is by teaching, preaching, and healing every disease (verse 23). At the Gospel's end he receives the authority he refused to take here (28:18).

The first word of Jesus' public preaching in Matthew is “Repent” (verse 17), the same call John made (3:2). Metanoia is a turning of mind and life toward God because his reign is near, and the fishermen's leaving of nets, boat, and father shows what turning looks like in a life.

Jesus begins in Galilee of the Gentiles and calls fishermen to become fishers of men. The mission that ends with “make disciples of all nations” (28:19) starts at the edge of Israel among ordinary workers, and the crowds from the Decapolis and Syria in verses 24 and 25 hint at its reach.

words.note: Peirazō, to test or to tempt. It occurs about thirty-nine times in the New Testament, six in Matthew. BDAG treats as distinct senses the testing that proves someone and the enticement to do wrong; context decides, and here both are present. The Spirit leads Jesus into the wilderness ‘to be tempted’ (verse 1), and the devil is called ho peirazōn, ‘the tempter’ (verse 3). The same verb is used of Jesus' opponents who come ‘to test’ him (16:1, 19:3, 22:35), so the contest begun in the wilderness continues through the Gospel. Its compound ekpeirazō, ‘put to the test’ (verse 7), comes from Deuteronomy 6:16.

Diabolos, slanderer, accuser, and so the devil. It occurs about thirty-seven times in the New Testament, four in this chapter. The Septuagint used it to translate Hebrew satan, adversary (Job 1:6, Zechariah 3:1), and in the Pastoral Letters the plural can describe human slanderers (1 Timothy 3:11). Matthew moves between diabolos and the transliterated Satanas (verse 10) without distinction. The Gospels present the devil as a personal adversary of God and his people, not merely a symbol for human evil, while never granting him equal standing with God.

Pterugion, literally ‘little wing’, a diminutive of pteryx, wing. It occurs only twice in the New Testament, here and in Luke 4:9. In the Septuagint it can mean the tip or edge of something, such as the fins of fish (Leviticus 11:9) or the corner of a garment (Ruth 3:9). Applied to the temple it means a projecting edge or corner of the walls, not the pointed spire the English word ‘pinnacle’ may suggest. Hegesippus uses the same word for the place from which James the Just was thrown (Eusebius, Church History 2.23).

Proskyneō, to bow down, prostrate oneself, worship. It occurs about sixty times in the New Testament, thirteen in Matthew and twenty-four in Revelation. It can describe homage to a human superior (18:26) as well as worship of God. Matthew uses it of the Magi before the child (2:2, 11), of the devil's demand (verse 9), in Jesus' reply (verse 10), and of the disciples worshiping the risen Jesus on the mountain in Galilee (28:17). Jesus refuses to bow to the devil and later receives proskynēsis himself, a quiet claim about who he is.

Metanoeō, to repent, change one's mind and direction. It occurs about thirty-four times in the New Testament, five in Matthew and twelve in Revelation. In classical Greek it could mean a change of opinion or regret; in the Septuagint and the Gospels it takes on the Hebrew sense of shuv, turning back to God. Jerome's Latin paenitentiam agite, ‘do penance’, shaped centuries of Western usage until Erasmus and then Luther, in the first of his Ninety-Five Theses (1517), argued that the Greek calls for a change of heart rather than an act of penance.

Akoloutheō, to follow, go after, and so to be a disciple. It occurs about ninety times in the New Testament, twenty-five in Matthew. It can describe crowds walking behind Jesus (verse 25) as well as committed disciples (verses 20 and 22), and Matthew uses both senses so that the reader must ask which kind of following is taking place. Jesus' call in verse 19 uses a different expression, deute opisō mou, literally ‘come after me’, the language of a servant or disciple walking behind a master.

Euangelion, good news, gospel. It occurs about seventy-six times in the New Testament, mostly in Paul, and four times in Matthew, three of them in the phrase ‘the gospel of the kingdom’ (4:23, 9:35, 24:14). In the Greek world the word announced good news such as a victory, and the Priene calendar inscription of 9 BC calls the birthday of Augustus the beginning of good tidings for the world. Isaiah's related verb announces God's return to reign (Isaiah 40:9, 52:7). Jesus' gospel is the news that God's kingdom, not Caesar's, has drawn near.

Anachōreō, to withdraw, go away. It occurs about fourteen times in the New Testament, ten of them in Matthew, who uses it for the Magi going home by another route (2:12), Joseph's flight to Egypt and then to Galilee (2:14, 22), and Jesus' withdrawals in the face of hostility (12:15, 14:13). In verse 12 it signals that John's arrest is a threat; Jesus withdraws, but into the region where his public work begins. Withdrawal in Matthew is never retreat from the mission; it is the way the mission moves to its appointed place.

christ:
The temptation shows who the Son is by showing what he refuses. Each test invites Jesus to use his sonship for himself or to secure the Father's promises by a shortcut. He will not turn stones to bread for his own hunger, though he will later feed five thousand and four thousand in the wilderness for others (14:13-21, 15:32-39); he answers, “Man shall not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of God” (verse 4, from Deuteronomy 8:3), the lesson God taught Israel through the manna. He will not force God's hand by a spectacular leap, though Psalm 91 promises the angels' protection; he answers, “Do not put the Lord your God to the test” (verse 7, from Deuteronomy 6:16), recalling Massah, where Israel demanded proof that the LORD was among them (Exodus 17:7). He will not take the kingdoms of the world by bowing to the devil; he answers, “Worship the Lord your God and serve Him only” (verse 10, from Deuteronomy 6:13). He is the true Israel, the Son who lives by trust where the nation lived by complaint, and he is also the second Adam, as Irenaeus saw (Against Heresies 5.21), undoing by obedience in a wilderness what the first man lost in a garden.

The same temptations return at the end. At the cross the mockers say, “If You are the Son of God, come down from the cross” (27:40), the exact words of the tempter, and again he refuses to save himself. He had told Peter that he could call more than twelve legions of angels (26:53); he does not, just as he would not leap from the temple to summon them. The kingdoms offered on the mountain are given to him on another mountain after the resurrection, when he says, “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me” (28:18). The difference is the road between: the devil offered glory without the cross, and the Father gives it through the cross. That is why Hebrews can say that we have one “who was tempted in every way that we are, yet was without sin” (Hebrews 4:15), and why the angels who come to serve him at the end of the testing (verse 11) are a sign that the Father's care, which Jesus would not force, was never absent.

The second half of the chapter shows the Son as the light Isaiah promised. In Isaiah the light dawns on Zebulun and Naphtali because a child is born to sit on David's throne and rule with justice and peace forever (Isaiah 9:6-7). Matthew quotes only the first two verses but assumes the rest: the Davidic son whose birth he narrated in chapter 1 is now the light rising over Galilee. His word for the light's rising, aneteilen (verse 16), is the verb of the star rising in Numbers 24:17 in the Greek Bible, and its noun is the ‘east’ or ‘rising’ where the Magi saw the star (2:2). He calls disciples as God once called prophets, with authority and without explanation, and promises to make them fishers of people, echoing Jeremiah 16:16, where the LORD sends fishermen to catch his people, there in a setting of judgment, and turning the image toward a gathering for the kingdom. His healing of every disease and sickness shows the kingdom already at work, and it fulfills in advance Isaiah's word that Matthew will quote in 8:17: “He took on our infirmities and carried our diseases.” The link between Isaiah 9 and Jesus is a claim of fulfillment, not only a thematic echo: Matthew believes the child of Isaiah 9 is Jesus, while Jewish interpreters have read the oracle differently, as the hard questions below explain.
interpretation:
The church read the temptation from early on as the second Adam's victory. Irenaeus of Lyon (Against Heresies 5.21, around 180) set it at the center of his teaching of recapitulation: the enemy who overcame Adam through food was overcome by a hungry man who answered from the law. Augustine (Harmony of the Gospels 2.16) addressed the different order in Matthew and Luke and judged it of no importance, since both report what truly happened and the evangelists did not always narrate in sequence. Gregory the Great's Lenten homily (Homilies on the Gospels 16, 591) matched the three temptations to gluttony, vainglory, and avarice, the means by which the serpent overcame the first man, and many medieval writers linked them to the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life (1 John 2:16). Thomas Aquinas asked why Christ willed to be tempted and discussed the order of the temptations (Summa Theologiae III, question 41).

Matthew 4:1-11 has been the Gospel for the first Sunday of Lent in the Western church for well over a thousand years, and it gave the season its shape of forty days. The Latin name of the Sunday, Invocabit, comes from the first word of its entrance chant, taken from Psalm 91:15, the very psalm the devil quoted, so that the church answered the tempter's misuse of Psalm 91 by singing the psalm's own promise. Luther's Invocavit sermons of March 1522, preached in Wittenberg to restrain violent reform, take their name from that Sunday. The Revised Common Lectionary reads the temptation on the first Sunday in Lent in Year A, paired with the temptation in Eden (Genesis 2:15-17, 3:1-7) and Paul's contrast of Adam and Christ (Romans 5:12-19), and reads 4:12-23 on the third Sunday after the Epiphany with Isaiah 9:1-4.

Modern study has read the scene through its Scriptures. Birger Gerhardsson (The Testing of God's Son, 1966) argued that the story is an early Christian midrash on Deuteronomy 6 to 8 structured by the Shema. In rabbinic interpretation (m. Berakhot 9:5) loving God with all one's heart means with both inclinations, with all one's soul means even at the cost of life, and with all one's might means with all one's wealth; Gerhardsson matched the bread to the heart, the leap from the temple to the soul, and the kingdoms to one's might, so that Jesus is the Son who loves God with all three. Dale Allison (The New Moses, 1993) collected the Mosaic patterns in Matthew's opening chapters, among them the forty days and forty nights and the mountain from which the land is shown, as the LORD showed Moses the whole land from Mount Nebo (Deuteronomy 34:1-4). Fyodor Dostoevsky's Grand Inquisitor, in The Brothers Karamazov (1880), turned the three temptations into a critique of any church that would rule people by bread, miracle, and authority rather than free faith.

The Galilee section has had its own history. Jewish interpreters read Isaiah 8:23 to 9:6 in its eighth-century setting. The Babylonian Talmud records the tradition that God wished to make Hezekiah the Messiah and did not because Hezekiah failed to sing praise (b. Sanhedrin 94a), and Rashi and other medieval commentators read the child of Isaiah 9 as Hezekiah. Targum Jonathan on Isaiah, however, calls the child the Messiah in whose days peace will increase (Targum Isaiah 9:5), showing that the oracle was read messianically in Jewish tradition too. Modern historians of Galilee, among them Mark Chancey (2002), have corrected an older Christian habit, influential in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, of describing Galilee as a half-pagan land in order to separate Jesus from Judaism; the region was Jewish, and Matthew's phrase is a scriptural label, not a census. The call of the fishermen has shaped the church's language of vocation and mission from the patristic period to the present, and Kingsbury's reading of 4:17 as a structural hinge (1975) remains a standard point of reference.

In art the temptation has been painted as a drama of three places. Duccio's panel from the Maestà (1308 to 1311, now in the Frick Collection) shows the kingdoms as small walled cities at Jesus' feet on the mountain, Matthew's climax. Ivan Kramskoi's Christ in the Desert (1872, Tretyakov Gallery, Moscow) shows a solitary, exhausted Jesus seated on bare rock, a picture of the inner struggle rather than the devil's offers, and Stanley Spencer began a series of forty paintings titled Christ in the Wilderness in 1939, one for each day of Lent, and finished eight, each showing Jesus alone among the creatures and hills. The calling of the first disciples appears in Duccio's Calling of Peter and Andrew (National Gallery of Art, Washington) and in countless later works.
text:
A few differences between English Bibles come from the manuscripts. In verse 10 many later manuscripts, including most of the Byzantine tradition, read ‘Get behind me, Satan’ (hypage opisō mou), probably borrowed from Jesus' words to Peter in 16:23; the earliest manuscripts and the Greek text behind the King James Version have only ‘Go away, Satan’, which the KJV renders ‘Get thee hence, Satan’. In verse 17 the Old Syriac manuscripts (Sinaitic and Curetonian) lack ‘Repent, for’, so that Jesus' preaching begins with ‘the kingdom of heaven is near’; the Greek manuscripts are united in including the call to repent, and all modern versions print it. In verse 18 the Greek of the earliest manuscripts says only ‘walking by the sea’; the name Jesus is supplied by modern translations for clarity and is present in later manuscripts, as in the KJV. Verse 13 spells Jesus' hometown Nazara in the earliest manuscripts, a form found also in Luke 4:16, where later copies have the more familiar Nazareth.

The quotation in verses 15 and 16 follows neither the Hebrew nor the Septuagint exactly. Where Isaiah has ‘the people walking in darkness’, Matthew has ‘the people sitting in darkness’ in the Greek (BSB “living”), wording closer to Psalm 107:10, “Some sat in darkness and in the shadow of death”. Matthew also trims Isaiah's contrast of former humiliation and future honor and keeps only the list of places. The oracle is numbered differently in Hebrew and English Bibles: the verse naming Zebulun, Naphtali, and Galilee of the nations is Isaiah 9:1 in English Bibles but 8:23 in the Hebrew Bible, and the people who walked in darkness are 9:2 in English but 9:1 in Hebrew, so every verse of Isaiah 9 is one number lower in a Jewish translation.

Translation choices also differ. In verse 24 the King James Version reads ‘lunatick’, following the Greek's ‘moonstruck’; modern versions render the sense, ‘epileptics’ (NASB) or ‘those having seizures’ (BSB). In verse 17 older versions say ‘the kingdom of heaven is at hand’ and many modern ones ‘has come near’; the Greek perfect ēngiken can be read either as near in time or as already arriving, and interpreters differ on how much of each to hear. In verse 19 the traditional ‘fishers of men’ is rendered in some recent versions as ‘fish for people’ (NRSV); the Greek anthrōpōn is generic and includes women.

teach.big: The beloved Son proves faithful where Israel failed by trusting and obeying his Father's word rather than grasping power, and then he begins, in a despised borderland, to call people to turn to God's near kingdom and to follow him.

outline.t: The Spirit leads the Son into testing; hunger is real, and Jesus refuses to use his power for himself because life depends on every word from God's mouth.
Trust does not demand proof: quoting a promise in order to force God's hand is testing him, and the devil's selective use of Psalm 91 warns every reader of the Bible.
The deepest temptation is to gain the right thing by bowing to the wrong master; Jesus will receive all authority by the cross, not by a shortcut, and the Father's care arrives when the test is over.

When the forerunner is silenced, Jesus begins in Galilee of the nations; God's light rises first on those who sat longest in darkness, and the message is the same call to repent because the kingdom is near.
Jesus calls ordinary workers in the middle of their work, and following him means leaving what defined them, trade and family, to be made into gatherers of people.
The kingdom comes as teaching, proclamation, and healing together, and its reach already extends beyond Israel's borders to Syria and the Decapolis.

teach.pitfalls:
Several misreadings are common. The first turns the temptation into a technique, as if quoting the right verse were a weapon that works by itself. Jesus answers with Scripture, but the devil quotes Scripture too; the difference is a heart that trusts and obeys the God who spoke, and the verses Jesus chooses are about exactly that. The second treats the story only as a moral example and misses what Matthew is doing: Jesus is the faithful Son who does for Israel, and for us, what we could not, and his victory is a gift before it is a pattern. The third reads the chapter as a list of forbidden things (bread, safety, success) and misses that each was good in itself; the temptation lies in the means and the master, not the desire.

With the second half, avoid making Galilee of the Gentiles a picture of a pagan land, a reading once used to separate Jesus from Judaism; Galilee was Jewish, and the phrase is Isaiah's. Avoid preaching the call of the fishermen as if it required every disciple to abandon family or work; these men were called to a particular apostolic role, and Jesus elsewhere sends healed people home (Mark 5:19). The call does require that every loyalty be reordered under his. Finally, avoid presenting verse 23 as a promise that faith will always bring healing; Matthew summarizes what happened as the kingdom arrived, not a guarantee of how it will come to each sick person before the resurrection.
teach.pastoral: The temptation speaks to people who are ashamed of being tempted. Being tested is not sin, and Jesus was tempted when he was hungry, alone, and physically weak; teachers can say plainly that temptation is not evidence that God has abandoned someone. The story also touches people who have been told that their suffering means God has withdrawn his favor, since the Spirit led the beloved Son into the wilderness immediately after the Father's word of love. The call of the fishermen can wound people whose families have been fractured, or who feel guilt over parents they could not care for; the text is not a license to neglect family, and Jesus later condemns those who use religion to evade caring for their parents (15:3-6). Those who are chronically ill or disabled should not hear verse 24 as a rebuke of their faith.

hard.q: Matthew and Luke give the temptations in a different order. Does that show the story was invented, and did Jesus really stand on a mountain from which all the kingdoms could be seen?
hard.a:
The objection runs as follows. Matthew orders the tests bread, temple, mountain; Luke orders them bread, mountain, temple. If both describe one event, at least one has changed the order, and critics argue that such freedom shows the evangelists were composing theology rather than reporting. David Friedrich Strauss (The Life of Jesus, 1835) treated the whole scene as a myth assembled from the testings of Israel, Moses, and Elijah, and noted that no mountain on earth shows all the kingdoms of the world, so the scene cannot be literal. Rudolf Bultmann (The History of the Synoptic Tradition, 1921) called it a legend shaped in early Christian debates over the use of Scripture. The skeptic adds that no one else was present, so the story rests on nothing anyone could have witnessed.

Responses take several forms. Augustine (Harmony of the Gospels 2.16) already noticed the difference and judged that it did not matter which temptation came second so long as all truly took place, since the evangelists did not always narrate in chronological sequence. Most modern scholars, including Joseph Fitzmyer in his Luke commentary, think Matthew's order is the earlier and that Luke moved the temple to the end to suit his Jerusalem-centered story; a minority think Luke's order came first. On either view the rearrangement is an evangelist's arrangement of a shared tradition, not a contradiction in what was said. On the mountain, John Calvin in his Harmony of the Gospels (1555) judged that the showing of all the kingdoms fits a vision better than any other explanation, and Matthew's own words, that the devil ‘showed’ Jesus all the kingdoms and their glory, allow that reading. On the question of witnesses, defenders note that the story has the form of an experience Jesus himself would have had to relate, and that it is told in thoroughly Jewish terms as a replay of Deuteronomy 6 to 8. Birger Gerhardsson (1966) studied it as early Christian midrash, a judgment about its form that leaves open whether it rests on Jesus' own account. Historians who reject the possibility of a personal devil will read it as symbolic narrative; the church has read it as the report of a real contest, and the dispute turns as much on worldview as on evidence.

hard.q: Is Matthew fair to Isaiah? Isaiah 9 seems to speak of the Assyrian crisis and a king of Judah, not of Jesus.
hard.a:
The objection has strong defenders. Read in its setting, Isaiah 8:23 to 9:6 (9:1-7 in English Bibles) addresses the Assyrian conquest of Israel's northern territories in 734 to 732 BC and promises that the humiliated regions will be honored when a royal child brings liberation. Jewish tradition identified that child with Hezekiah: the Babylonian Talmud reports that God wished to make Hezekiah the Messiah (b. Sanhedrin 94a), and Rashi, Ibn Ezra, and Radak read the chapter of Hezekiah's reign. Historical-critical commentators on Isaiah generally agree that the oracle first celebrated the birth or accession of a Judean king. On this view Matthew has lifted a few lines out of context because they mention Galilee, the kind of proof-texting Jewish critics of Christianity, from the Middle Ages to the present, have often charged the Gospels with.

Responses start from the oracle itself. Isaiah promises a child on David's throne whose government and peace will have no end and who will reign “from that time and forevermore” (Isaiah 9:7), names that exceed any king of Judah, Hezekiah included, whose kingdom was overrun by Sennacherib in 701 BC. Targum Jonathan, an Aramaic Jewish rendering, calls the child the Messiah in whose days peace will increase (Targum Isaiah 9:5), so the messianic reading is not a Christian invention. Richard Hays (Echoes of Scripture in the Gospels, 2016) and others argue that Matthew's fulfillment quotations point to whole passages and patterns, not isolated words: by quoting the opening of the oracle Matthew invokes its promise of the Davidic child, whom he has already presented in chapter 1, and its geography fits the place where Jesus actually began. The verb plēroō, to fill full, in Matthew often means that a pattern in Israel's story reaches its fullness (as with Hosea 11:1 in 2:15) rather than that a prediction is checked off. Jewish and Christian readers will continue to disagree about the child's identity; what both can grant is that Matthew is reading Isaiah as a whole book of promise, not as a list of place names.

observe: What are the three things the devil asks Jesus to do, and which verse from Deuteronomy does Jesus answer with each time?
How does the devil's quotation of Psalm 91 differ from the psalm itself, and what is left out?
What do the two pairs of brothers leave behind in verses 20 and 22, and how quickly do they leave?
interpret: Why do the first two temptations begin with ‘If You are the Son of God’, and how do Jesus' answers show what kind of Son he is?
Why might Matthew see special meaning in Jesus beginning his ministry in Galilee of the Gentiles rather than in Jerusalem?
How does the offer of all the kingdoms of the world in verse 8 connect with Jesus' words at the end of the Gospel in 28:18?
apply: Each temptation offered something good by the wrong means. Where are you tempted to reach for a good thing by a shortcut or by bowing to the wrong master?
The devil quoted Scripture too. How can you tell when the Bible is being used to serve someone's own ends, including your own?
What would following Jesus require you to leave, loosen, or hold differently this year?
